opus-5.5.text:
I think the comparison to CUDA is useful, but mostly as a reminder of what actually made CUDA matter, not as a slogan.

When people look back at CUDA, they often see the end state: a dominant platform that everyone builds on. But if you look at how it got there, it was a very long, patient investment. For years it was not obvious that general-purpose GPU computing would pay off. What made it work was that it solved a real pain for developers, it was consistent and reliable, and NVIDIA kept supporting it even when the usage was small. Then, when deep learning arrived, the foundation was already there.

So when I think about something like world foundation models for physical AI, the CUDA analogy shapes our decisions in a few ways.

First, you have to think about who your developers are and what problem they cannot solve without you. In physical AI, robotics and autonomous vehicles, the bottleneck is data. You cannot easily collect enough real-world data covering all the rare and dangerous situations. A world model that can generate physically plausible video, and that people can post-train for their own robot or their own car, addresses that directly. If it doesn't solve that pain, nobody will build on it, no matter how impressive the demo looks.

Second, openness and accessibility matter a lot. CUDA succeeded because researchers and students could just use it. That's part of why we release models, code, and tools openly, so the community can fine-tune them, break them, and tell us what's missing. A platform only becomes a platform when other people build things you never imagined.

Third, it means accepting that the payoff is long term. Today these models are still far from perfect. Physics is sometimes wrong, object permanence fails, long-horizon consistency is hard. If you judged only by this year's results, you might give up. But the bet is that physical AI will be a very large field, and the tools that are ready when it takes off will matter enormously.

And finally, it keeps us humble. Calling something "the next CUDA" is not something you declare; it's something the developers decide by choosing to use it. So day to day, the guide is quite practical: make the models better, make them easier to adapt, listen to the people using them, and keep investing even when the curve still looks flat.

r001.rationale: It treats CUDA as a lesson in sustained investment and solving real developer needs, and says its success is not a slogan to copy.

r002.rationale: It says to start with developers’ unsolved problems and warns that a model will not attract users if it does not solve a real pain, conveying a problem-first approach.

fable-5.1.text:
I think about it less as an ambition and more as a discipline, because "building the next CUDA" is a sentence that sounds grand and means almost nothing unless you ask what CUDA actually did. CUDA didn't win because it was a great piece of software in year one. It won because NVIDIA kept investing in it for roughly a decade before the payoff was obvious, and because every year it got a little easier for a developer to do something they couldn't do before. The moat was accumulated developer trust, not any single feature.

So when I use that as a guide for decisions today, it pushes me toward a few things.

First, it makes me suspicious of anything that only makes sense if we're right about the timeline. If the only justification for a project is "in two years everyone will need this," that's a bet, not a platform. A platform decision should still look reasonable if the world moves slower than we think. CUDA was useful for scientific computing long before deep learning showed up. That's the test I apply: is this valuable to someone right now, even if the big wave is late?

Second, it makes me think about the layer. CUDA sits at a very particular level of abstraction, low enough to be general, high enough that people can actually build on it. For physical AI, the equivalent question is what the "primitive" is. I don't think it's a single robot or a single model. I think it's something closer to world simulation and world models, the ability to generate and reason about physically plausible futures. If you get that layer right, you let a thousand companies build things you never imagined. If you get it wrong, you've built a product, which is fine, but it's not a platform.

Third, and this is the part people underestimate, it pushes you toward being boring for a long time. Documentation, tooling, backward compatibility, not breaking people's code. None of that is exciting, and all of it is what turns a research artifact into infrastructure. When I look at a decision and ask "does this make it easier for an outside developer to depend on us for five years," that's the CUDA question. A lot of good research fails that test, and that's okay, but you have to know which thing you're doing.

The honest caveat is that you can't fully plan a CUDA. There was a lot of luck in it, and a lot of patience from leadership that most organizations wouldn't tolerate. So I try not to treat it as a blueprint. I treat it as a reminder that the valuable thing is usually the thing that compounds slowly, and that the temptation to chase whatever is loud this quarter is exactly the temptation you have to resist.

r001.rationale: The candidate says CUDA should be a reminder, not a blueprint, and argues that a project must have value now even if the anticipated wave arrives late. Past CUDA success alone is not presented as sufficient justification.

r002.rationale: The candidate cautions against relying on a predicted timeline and discusses choosing the right platform layer, but does not clearly warn against choosing problems to fit a predetermined solution.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a useful ambition, but it’s not specific enough to guide a decision by itself. You have to ask: What problem are we solving today? Who needs it? And why would they choose to build on what we provide?

The danger is that you start by trying to create an ecosystem. I would start with something that delivers clear value for a developer, even if the initial use case is narrow. Then you learn which parts need to become more general. If you build the abstraction too early, you can end up making something elegant that nobody needs.

So I would use “the next CUDA” as a long-term direction. It encourages you to think about compatibility, developer experience, and whether other people can build things you didn’t anticipate. But the immediate decisions still have to be grounded in a real workload and a real user. What makes their work substantially easier today? That’s where I would start.

r001.rationale: It says “the next CUDA” is too nonspecific to guide a decision by itself and should be grounded in a real workload and user.

r002.rationale: It recommends starting from a real user need and cautions against creating an ecosystem or abstraction before validating the problem.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s useful as a long-term ambition, but it’s not specific enough to guide every decision today. You have to ask: What problem are we solving for developers? What can we make dramatically easier or faster? And why would someone choose to build on our platform?

The ambition should push us to think beyond a single product—to think about tools, compatibility, and the experience of building something that works reliably. But we still need a concrete starting point. Solve an important problem extremely well, earn developers’ trust, and expand from there. You don’t get an ecosystem just by deciding you want one.

r001.rationale: The response says the ambition alone is not specific enough to guide every decision, but it does not address whether past CUDA success justifies pursuing a similar ambition today.

r002.rationale: The response recommends starting with an important problem, but does not clearly caution against choosing problems to fit a predetermined solution.
